content.overview: Section 34 of the Specific Relief Act, 1963 allows any person entitled to a legal character, or to any right as to any property, to sue a person who denies or is interested to deny that title, for a declaration that he is so entitled. The plaintiff need not ask for any further relief. The proviso says no court shall make such a declaration where the plaintiff, being able to seek further relief than a mere declaration of title, omits to do so. The declaration is discretionary. It is not specific performance and not an injunction.
content.study: Plead a legal character or a property right, and a defendant who denies it. If further relief is available and is not asked, the proviso blocks a bare declaration. Do not use section 34 to enforce a contract.

learningObjectives: State who may seek a section 34 declaration.
Apply the proviso on omitted further relief.
Keep declaration distinct from specific performance.
enhancement.definition: Section 34 is a discretionary declaration of a legal character or a property right against a person who denies or is interested to deny it.
enhancement.legalPrinciple: A declaration is available without further relief only if the plaintiff could not seek further relief. The proviso is mandatory where further relief was available and omitted.
essentialIngredients: Legal character or a right as to property
Defendant denies or is interested to deny it
Further relief asked if the plaintiff is able to seek it
enhancement.detailedExplanation: The entitlement is present tense: a person entitled to a legal character or to a right as to any property. The defendant must deny, or be interested to deny, the title. The court may in its discretion make the declaration. The opening words say the plaintiff need not ask for further relief, but the proviso qualifies that. If the plaintiff is able to seek further relief than a mere declaration of title and omits to do so, the court shall not make the declaration. Further relief means a relief the plaintiff could have sought in the suit, such as possession where the plaintiff is out of possession. A plaintiff in possession seeking a declaration against a denial is the ordinary case outside the proviso. Section 34 does not order a contract to be performed.
examples: A person in possession of a house sues a stranger who denies his title, and asks only for a declaration. Section 34 can be considered.
A plaintiff out of possession asks only for a declaration of title and does not ask for possession. The proviso applies if possession could have been sought.
A buyer asks for a declaration that a sale contract exists, without seeking performance. That is not the section 10 remedy.
enhancement.problemApplication: Identify the character or property right, the denial, and whether further relief was available. If it was available and omitted, refuse the bare declaration.
distinctions: Bare declaration vs declaration with further relief
Legal character vs a mere commercial hope
enhancement.caseLawNotes: No new case citation or ratio was added. Ready-and-willing and adequate-relief readings remain on the case-law gate.

The defendant must deny or be interested to deny it.
Further relief must be asked if it could be sought.
Section 34 does not enforce a contract.
